cells.tense: The small thing you keep returning to is lit, and coming back to it is a choice you're making.
cells.ask: Start something new this week with only a rough sense of where it goes, and keep at it for exactly one week before deciding whether it's working.
cells.core:
The small thing you return to is still going, and it's held up by you coming back to it rather than by any enthusiasm that happened to pass through. Alone with it, you're not shut off from people — the practice seems to keep you in contact with things, and the refining stays pointed at getting better rather than at getting safe.

What happens next here isn't something you'd have planned, and you don't have to arrange it. Begin something with only a rough idea of where it goes, and give it a week before you decide anything. What you're already carrying doesn't need defending; it needs the company of one thing you can't yet see the end of.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one choosing to come back to it.
cells.verb: keeping one small practice lit through repetition
cells.place: the place where you move without seeing the whole road

cells.tense: You're braced for what happens if you stop, and the stopping hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Finish one piece of the practice at a clean stopping point — not at your best, just done — and leave it closed for a full day.
cells.core:
You keep tightening the practice against a morning that hasn't come. Somewhere ahead is the version where it all comes apart, and the rehearsing is using up the thing you're rehearsing to protect. Being alone with it stopped feeling like a choice somewhere back there and started feeling like the only safe room, so the door stays shut and the surface doesn't quite get smooth enough to set down.

There is a finish you can walk to on purpose. Take one piece of it to a clean stopping point — not your best, just done — and leave it closed for a whole day. Ending it yourself, while it's still up, is the part the bracing isn't letting you have.
cells.sheetLine: The refining keeps the ending somewhere other than here.

cells.tense: Starting the thing and keeping it going has felt like a risk, and you've stopped reaching for it.
cells.ask: Do ten minutes of the thing today and stop on purpose, before it feels finished or good, then walk away without adding anything to it.
cells.core:
Keeping something going has felt like a risk for long enough that you've stopped reaching for it, and what's left is a doorway you've learned to walk past. This isn't laziness or a missing gift — it's a habit of holding back from the very thing that would steady you, and it shows in how quickly you set things down.

Ten minutes today, then stop on purpose before it feels done or good. Walking away on your own terms is the part that's been missing, and that's what you're practicing — not the thing itself. It gets to stay small and unimpressive while you do it.
cells.sheetLine: Ten minutes, stopped on purpose, is the whole assignment.
cells.verb: keeping one small practice lit through repetition
cells.place: the place where you move without seeing the whole road

cells.tense: The practice is already running through your days, and you describe it as though it happens on its own.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person, once, that you have gotten good at something through your own repetition — naming it plainly, without calling it luck or a natural gift.
cells.core:
Your hands already know how to come back to this — the timing, the refining, the small things you'd not bother explaining — and you call it just how you are, or something that arrived on its own. The work has been happening. What hasn't happened is you saying it's yours. Notice how readily the ability gets explained as a quirk of who you are rather than something you built turn by turn.

Tell one person, once, that you've gotten good at this through repetition. Naming it plainly, without dressing it as luck or a natural gift, is the whole move. The work is already done; only the saying-so is missing.
cells.sheetLine: You built it. You keep calling it a quirk.

attempts.check: The record supports that practice is steady and chosen, but it doesn't say the person knows it's working as well as they do — I've put 'you know it' near the front, and a reader could reasonably say they'd never call it knowing. The ask survives being wrong either way: starting something before the picture is clear is useful whether or not this is already balanced. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you know it' — it flatters the read and guesses at their inner accounting. I'll move the knowing to the outside where it can be seen and drop the claim about their awareness of it.
